title: 5 Ways to Improve Any Team This Year
author: Samuel Crome
summary: Samuel Crome offers five low-workload adjustments school teams can make at the start of the year: creating clarity around a small number of goals to counter leaders' 'transmission illusion' (overestimating how much staff remember from a single announcement), reducing procedural friction the way digital marketers minimize 'clicks to purchase,' mastering systems through frequent short debriefs and scenario-based stress tests rather than waiting for a big data drop, actually working together in subgroups on shared problems rather than just discussing them in meetings, and prioritizing team-specific learning tied to concrete goals rather than generic whole-staff CPD. His scenario example, walking a Senior Leadership Team through what happens when a student wanders the corridor after being sent out of a lesson, is offered as a way to surface hidden variance in how staff actually interpret shared policies. Throughout, Crome frames these as incremental adjustments rather than added workload, explicitly applicable to any team in any school.
points: Crome's 'transmission illusion' concept warns leaders that communicating a priority once or twice creates false confidence that staff remember it, arguing teams must overcommunicate a small number of goals repeatedly rather than announce many priorities once.

He borrows a digital-marketing concept, 'clicks to purchase,' to reframe team efficiency: identify and remove unnecessary procedural friction (excess emails, buried resources, redundant data entry) so more staff time goes to thinking rather than navigating barriers.

His debrief research citation is notably concrete: a focused debrief can take just 18 minutes, arguing teams should review processes in small frequent chunks rather than waiting for a major outcome like a termly data drop.

His scenario-based system-testing technique surfaces hidden disagreement: walking a leadership team through a concrete scenario (a student wandering the corridor after being removed from a lesson) exposes variance in how staff would actually respond, which abstract policy discussion conceals.
quotes: Research shows that leaders suffer from the 'transmission illusion', where we overestimate how much our staff know or remember, assuming they know more because we've communicated it once or twice.
Keep it slimmed down. Assume they will forget. Overcommunicate!
The aim is to identify where you are adding unnecessarily to people's workload. Remove friction, even just from one or two places, and increase thinking about the things that matter.

Debrief research suggests that we shouldn't wait until a big outcome to review something, but chop things up into chunks and review processes little and often. Research shows a focused debrief can take just 18 minutes!
Simply talking about systems or processes doesn't really work, because typical levels of groupthink or lack of psychological safety means that not everyone contributes freely.
Start with what your team's goals are this year, and then reverse engineer to work out which steps you'll need to take to reach them.
